Minimal Pairs Causal Experiment Report

Gemini 2.5 Flash (gdmorig) Preference Decomposition Across Numbers & Names Domains

📌 Executive Summary & Key Results

This report presents the causal evaluation of Gemini 2.5 Flash on Minimal Pairs datasets constructed via K-Means Non-Target Feature Space Stratification.

  • Logistic Regression Validation: The logistic regression predictions closely match the measured minimal pair causal win rates (MAE ~ 0.05-0.08, Pearson r > 0.85). This confirms that logistic regression accurately decomposes multi-feature confounding in pair preferences.
  • Causal Effect Invariance: Key preference drivers remain strong and invariant across all pair generation methodologies (Greedy, Greedy with Deduplication, K-Means Stratified):
    • Numbers: is_mult_10 (+31% to +35%), value (+17% to +24%), is_palindrome (+16% to +20%), is_prime (+11% to +19%).
    • Names: frac_2020 (+25% to +36%), female_frac (+18% to +21%), bouba_frac (+11% to +14%), census_freq (+14% to +19%).
  • Gender Control Analysis: In our initial observational experiment, randomly pairing within a gender-balanced pool resulted in same-gender pairs ~50% of the time. However, matching on non-target features without gender control shifted this balance—increasing the proportion of opposite-gender pairs for features like starting_vowel (since starting-vowel names skew ~65% female in Census data). To test whether this feature-induced gender mismatch affected confounding, we evaluate a variant that explicitly adds female_frac to non-target covariate matching (13 features total, reported in Section 4), demonstrating that controlling for gender resolves the starting_vowel confound.
1. Main Result: Measured Minimal Pair Effects vs. Logistic Regression Predictions

The figure below compares the measured causal win rates (from Gemini 2.5 Flash minimal pair evaluations, 25 pairs × ~50 prompts × 2 presentation orderings = 2,500 total evals per feature) against the predictions of the learned Logistic Regression model fit on the original dataset (as in Figure 1 of the main paper).

Figure 1: Comparison of Measured Minimal Pair Causal Effects (Blue) vs Logistic Regression Predictions (Red) for Numbers and Names (K-Means Stratified minimal pairs).
📊 Goodness of Fit & Model Calibration Note:
The Logistic Regression model (fit on observational pairs_circle data) accurately predicts minimal pair causal win rates in experimental settings:
  • Numbers Domain: Mean Absolute Error (MAE) = 0.051, Pearson r = 0.941.
  • Names Domain (K-Means): Mean Absolute Error (MAE) = 0.078, Pearson r = 0.884.
This close correspondence confirms that linear feature preferences accurately capture model behavior across both observational and counterfactual minimal pair evaluations.

3. Minimal Pair Generation Logic & Entity Pool Explainer

💡 Non-Target Feature Space Stratified Pairing Algorithm & Literature Context

Standard minimal pair selection can suffer from spatial clustering bias—where all 25 pairs for a feature are drawn from a single narrow sub-region of entity space (e.g. all sum_digits pairs being near centennial boundaries like 297 vs 301). Non-target feature space stratification extends classical non-parametric causal matching literature (e.g. Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983; Stuart, 2010) by replacing local greedy selection with uniform spatial coverage across non-target covariate space:

  1. Entity Candidate Pool:
    • Numbers Domain: All 1,000 integers between 0 and 999 (11 features computed for each).
    • Names Domain: Top 2,000 candidate names by Census 2020 frequency (with decade popularity features computed from SSA 1960–2020 data; 13–14 features computed for each).
    • Note on Zero Decade Popularities (frac_XXXX = 0): When a candidate name does not appear in a given SSA decade top-1,000 table (1960, 1980, 2000, or 2020), its popularity feature frac_XXXX is assigned 0.0. Because the minimum recorded popularity for names present on the SSA tables is extremely small (ranging from ≈ 1.38 × 10-5 or 0.00138% of births in 1960 to ≈ 5.89 × 10-5 in 2020), assigning 0.0 serves as a close numerical approximation for unlisted rare names rather than introducing missing NaN values into covariate matching and logistic regression modeling.
  2. Target Feature Separation: To ensure paired entities (e1, e2) differ substantially on the target feature, the candidate entity pool is partitioned into two distinct target pools:
    • Continuous Features: High Target (top quartile, > 75th percentile) vs. Low Target (bottom quartile, < 25th percentile).
    • Binary Features: True vs. False target value pools.
  3. Non-Target Feature Scaling & K-Means Clustering: All non-target features are min-max scaled to [0, 1]D. Candidate cross-pool pairs (e1 ∈ High, e2 ∈ Low) are clustered into K=25 clusters using their midpoints in non-target feature space.
  4. Confound Distance Minimization & Set-Based Deduplication: Within each cluster k ∈ {1, ..., 25}, candidate pairs are evaluated by Euclidean distance √(∑ (fi(e1) - fi(e2))2). To enforce entity uniqueness across all 25 pairs, a global used_entities tracking set is maintained. The algorithm greedily selects the pair (e1, e2) minimizing distance such that e1 ∉ used_entities and e2 ∉ used_entities, ensuring exactly 25 × 2 = 50 unique entities per target feature.
4. Alternate Pairing Methods & Multi-Method Comparison

Below is a direct comparison of causal effect sizes across different pair selection algorithms (K-Means Stratified vs. K-Means accounting for gender vs. Greedy vs. Greedy with Deduplication vs. Logistic Regression Predictions):

Figure 2: Multi-method comparison across Numbers and Names domains showing K-Means, K-Means (accounting for gender), Greedy, Greedy (with Deduplication), and Logistic Regression Predictions.

🔍 Explanations of Alternate Pairing Strategies

  • Greedy: Nearest-neighbor matching in non-target feature space across target-split pools (High vs Low / True vs False). Evaluates all candidate pairs across the two target pools and greedily selects the 25 pairs that minimize Euclidean distance in non-target feature space, allowing entity reuse across pairs. Minimal pairs generated this way can suffer from spatial clustering bias (drawn from narrow sub-regions of entity space).
  • Greedy (with Deduplication): Nearest-neighbor matching across target-split pools enforcing entity uniqueness (50 distinct entities per feature). Eliminates entity reuse bias but retains spatial clustering bias.
  • K-Means (accounting for gender): Evaluates K-Means non-target space stratification by explicitly adding female_frac to the 12 regression features (13 features total). In our initial setup, random pairing within a gender-balanced name pool yielded same-gender pairs ~50% of the time, but non-target feature matching shifted this probability toward opposite-gender pairs (e.g. for starting_vowel, which skews ~65% female). Adding gender to non-target covariate matching explicitly tests and controls for this feature-induced gender mismatch.
